column2: Photo by Arnold Newman: Pollock, 37, arms crossed, in paint-spattered work clothes in front of his eighteen-foot canvas Number 9. Headline: “Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?” The first recognition of the small downtown art world by the mainstream media. Bill jokes that Pollock looks like a gas-station attendant. an 18-foot canvas (≈5.5 m) Consequences: The New York School is consecrated by the media.

Opening of an exhibition of Anni Albers's textiles, announced by the New York Times; widely covered by the press (Interiors, Christian Science Monitor, New York Herald Tribune, Craft Horizons). coverage: Interiors 109 (Oct. 1949), “Power Behind the Loom”; Christian Science Monitor (Oct. 19, 1949), “Anni Albers' Textiles Serve, Not Dominate, Architecture”; Herald Tribune (Sept. 25, 1949), on hanging panels as flexible partitions Consequences: Anni Albers is consecrated as a textile artist in the United States

Fuller writes to Snelson to give him credit, in all his public lectures, for the original demonstration of the structural advantage of discontinuous compression and continuous tension, and hails him as a true pioneer who will one day be known. Letter dated December 22, 1949, Fuller Papers; mention of the “Energetic Geometry” Consequences: Establishes that the tension/compression structure came first from Snelson

Howe, Kahn's former partner, a resident at the American Academy in Rome since 1947, arrives at Yale on January 1, 1950, in the middle of the collaborative problem. Consequences: The Howe–Albers duo at the head of the art school.
A lecture given as part of the gallery program; Howe probably present, newly arrived.

A card typed at a slant to form a diamond, signed “love kk,” with two short poems (“These Days” and “The Day's Orders, Boys”) and a comment on Saroyan. Postmark “11 pm Jan 29 (?) 1950”; signature in lowercase “yrs, kk” with a Greek k

Albers keeps asking for the other 20% of what he calls his pension fund; the question remains a sore point for a long time. Minutes of the Board meeting of February 22, 1950 (?) Consequences: Albers's lasting resentment of the college

A fact-finding committee (Goldowski, Hetherington, and two students, Vera Williams and Andy Oates) writes a five-page report summarizing the two positions. A 5-page report Consequences: The two camps are formalized

After a St. Louis Browns–Washington Senators game (a 5-4 win in 12 innings), Olson sends Dawson an annotated, illustrated scorecard, mailed from Washington on June 3, 1950. card folded in two; Dawson's name written surname first (a play on Ostrowski, the Senators' outfielder); curved ink lines toward “YR BOYS” and “DID ALL RIGHT!”; a semicircle drawn with tiny words about Ostrowski and Michaels, second base Consequences: Dawson reads it as a visual message announcing The Rose of the World
Memorandum from Howe: working conditions can be described as intolerable — a complaint similar to Albers's
Albers writes that one of his conditions is that he be able to avoid most of the administration

Albers keeps in his collection of press clippings a New York Herald Tribune photograph showing about ninety sailboats seen from the air, massed on Long Island Sound for the start of Larchmont Race Week; it resembles his “schools of fish” exercise. About ninety sailboats; newspaper of July 16, 1950. Consequences: Illustrates his passion for “relatedness,” forms harmoniously linked.

Albers writes the college a furious one-sentence letter demanding that neither he nor his wife be mentioned in the publications of the college, which is holding his property and does not answer his letters. A one-sentence letter; another letter from Albers to the Board of January 17, 1952 Consequences: The final symbolic break between Albers and BMC

Albers, exasperated by the college's silence about his property, writes a one-sentence letter demanding that he and Anni no longer be mentioned in the college's publications Words: he and his wife do not wish to be mentioned in the publications of the college, which is holding his property and does not answer his letters Atmosphere: Final coldness Stakes: The artistic founder breaks with the institution

Malrey has roasted an enormous turkey ahead of time (she and Cornelia had the day off), helped by Mary Fiore and several students and teachers; Rumaker lays white sheets from the North Lodge linen as tablecloths and digs up stubby candles for each table (tablecloths and candles were never used, even for the dressed-up Saturday night chicken dinners); someone has gathered laurel, holly, pine boughs, and cones for the fireplace and the tables; T. J., the new handyman, brings the biggest Yule log ever seen, lit at dawn and burning ingot-red throughout the meal; wine and all the trimmings; Merrill deigns to come, pleasant after a few drinks, and then helps Rumaker with the dishes so they can go back up sooner white sheets, stubby candles, laurel/holly/pine/cones, a log filling the mouth of the big fieldstone fireplace, an enormous turkey, wine Consequences: That day Rumaker knows that BMC is now his home; he hurries back down with Merrill in the cold dusk to make love

Rumaker sets white sheets and candles on the tables; T. J. hauls in the biggest log ever seen, lit at dawn and burning ingot-red throughout the meal; turkey, wine, greenery on the mantel; Merrill, after a few drinks, becomes pleasant and then helps Rumaker with the dishes so they can go back up sooner; the two of them hurry up through the cold dusk, their breath steaming, toward the shack and the quilt Atmosphere: The glow of the candles and the log, the warmth of a family regained, worries about the college's future forgotten for a day Stakes: Rumaker recognizes BMC as his home; the idyll at its height — he has never been so happy

Life publishes the photograph of the fourteen men and the one woman (Hedda Sterne, placed so as to dominate the group), dubbed the “Irascibles Eighteen” by the Herald Tribune of May 23, 1950, dressed respectably, like bankers, at Newman's request. 14 men, 1 woman; 3 colleagues absent from the photo session.

Willem de Kooning writes the text “What Abstract Art Means to Me” for a symposium at MoMA, later published in the museum's Bulletin. Text published in The Bulletin of The Museum of Modern Art, pp. 4-5

On the occasion of the exhibition Abstract Painting and Sculpture in America (January 1951, with Excavation), de Kooning writes “What Abstract Art Means to Me” for the symposium and has his text read by Andrew Carnduff Ritchie, then director of MoMA's department of painting and sculpture: some painters, himself among them, have found that painting — any kind, any style of painting — to be painting at all, is a way of living today, a style of living. Text published in the MoMA Bulletin 18 (spring 1951).

Too excited to respect the boundaries of words, Olson opens his letter of March 17 with “christamiexcited”; further on, the “f” key of his typewriter breaks and unleashes a volley of curses that ironically culminates in “fuck it”. Words: “christamiexcited”; “fuck it” Atmosphere: Epistolary excitement, a writing fever under a foreign sky Stakes: Writing as a bodily flow, the machine itself taking part

The couple's Blueprints appear in a three-page article (“Speaking of Pictures”) in Life (pp. 22-24); they then contact their friends Liberman and Brodovitch to find work thanks to this sudden fame. Plenty of tempting promises, no work
The couple's “Blueprints” are featured in a three-page article in Life. pp. 22-24 of the magazine Consequences: quick fame, but no job obtained

Dawson and four friends (Carl, Tim, Webber, Joel) watch the Brooklyn Dodgers beat the Asheville Tourists (Class B) 9-8: Campanella (catcher) hits two home runs, Robinson (second base) an inside-the-park home run; Duke Snider chases a ball in center field and narrowly beats six kids swarming onto the field. The children cheer the Black players, most adults support the home team; a spectator makes racist remarks, and Joel, Tim, and Webber change seats. Black fans, denied seats, stand by the thousands along the left-field line; a tall Black woman runs to photograph each of Campanella's home runs and, at the third, tears off her hat, shrieking, and sets the stands roaring with laughter. score 9-8; Asheville 3 runs in the 1st, 4 in the 3rd, 1 in the 6th; Brooklyn 3 in the 4th, 3 in the 5th, 3 in the 7th; a 4-hour game; a ballpark of about 1500 seats, at least 5000 spectators, about one-sixth of them Black; back just in time for dinner

Inning by inning, Brooklyn comes back against Asheville and wins 9-8; at each of Campanella's home runs a tall Black woman rushes up to photograph him; at the second, she tears off her hat and falls back shrieking — the whole ballpark dies laughing; Snider fights six kids for a ball in center field; Joel, Tim, and Webber leave a racist neighbor to join Carl and Dawson; back just in time for dinner. Atmosphere: an exhausted, restless, hilarious crowd; four hours of sun Stakes: segregation cracked by sport and laughter

Life's “Speaking of Pictures” section publishes an article with photographs of Rauschenberg and Susan Weil's blueprint experiments. “Speaking of Pictures” section, Life, April 19, 1951 Consequences: Exhibited at MoMA the same year
An article with photographs of their blueprint experiments appears in Life's “Speaking of Pictures” section. Life, April 19, 1951, “Speaking of Pictures” section

In his letter of resignation, Leser writes that he found at BMC the genuinely democratic constitution and practice he had been looking for when he left Olivet; his departure is for purely personal reasons; he is in love with Black Mountain and feels it to be as it should be. Letter to the Board of April 24, 1951 Consequences: The departure of a beloved teacher

At a members-only session, Elaine says she believes more in van Gogh: a distorted look or figure is an irrational whim; Bill disapproves of distortion from the inside (the German Expressionists) as much as from the outside (Soutine, Bacon); Elaine recalls Vlaminck's remark: a telephone wire carrying emotion is painted with a wavy line seventeen male artists around her Consequences: an illustration of the self-assurance of Elaine, 33, the only woman among the men
Time magazine publishes an article dubbing de Kooning “Willem the Walloper,” p. 63.

Soon after his arrival, Shahn gives a captivating lecture in the dining hall in which he imagines the responses of a psychologist, a physicist, an art critic, and so on, to the same painting, to show how contingent the aspects of realism are; he defines realism as “an earnest search for truth within the framework of one's own values”. transcript preserved in the Black Mountain College Project Papers, Western Regional Archives, Asheville

Before the community gathered for a meal, Shahn improvises a series of imaginary views of a painting — psychologist, physicist, critic — and defines realism as an earnest search for truth within the framework of one's own values. Words: Realism as “an earnest search for truth within the framework of one's own values” Atmosphere: A captivating lecture, the ordinary dining room turned into a lecture hall Stakes: A social realist amid the abstract painters of summer 1951 (Motherwell)

Inspired by the exchange of glyphs, Olson asks his friend W. H. Ferry for funds for the college, arguing for the importance of artists from different disciplines working together in the America of 1951. Consequences: an attempt to raise money for the college
A letter from Imogen Cunningham to the couple, a trace of their friendship.

At the faculty meeting of November 2, 1951, Olson declares that he believes in the absolute freedom of the student, even the freedom to concentrate on a single subject. Minutes of the meetings of October-November 1951 Consequences: The educational debate of the new Black Mountain

At a faculty meeting, Huss remarks good-humoredly that Olson would make a poor member of the Community Council: his most valuable contribution is to raise things to a certain level of energy; Olson was “not so hot” as an administrator. Minutes of November 9, 1951; a joking tone, judging by the context Consequences: Debate on Olson's role in governance
Litz dances The Glyph in New York on December 23, 1951.

It has been snowing for two hours, and the temperature is falling. Olson wants to drain the radiator cock of his car and looks for a flashlight. In the dining hall, Twombly is playing music by Morton Feldman on the organ with three students (guitar, drums, piano); Twombly tells him there is a flashlight in Rauschenberg's car. Rauschenberg, who had been playing canasta at the farm, walks barefoot out of the dining hall and into the icy lake; Twombly follows him in up to his waist, six meters from the shore, then turns back; Rauschenberg turns around, Twombly guides him (“This way Bob”), Olson brings blankets and half carries him to the dining hall kitchen and warms him by the fire snowing for two hours, pitch-dark night, Twombly 20 feet from the shore (up to his hips), Rauschenberg toward the middle of the lake, moans and a voice catching, two flashlights, blankets, an electric stove, unfocused eyes, Olson feels the cold in his ankles as he goes to bed Consequences: Olson writes to Robert Creeley the next day; four men sitting in the kitchen ignore the scene, one smiling with satisfaction; a suicide attempt or a cry for attention, left unresolved

Snow and falling temperatures; Olson goes down to the dining hall for a flashlight to drain his radiator; Twombly and three students are pounding out Feldman's music (organ, guitar, drums, piano); too bad he wasn't there earlier, they were really tearing it up, now it is flattening out; the flashlight is in Rauschenberg's car; Rauschenberg, wound up from canasta, walks out barefoot, blown out by the pressure of the music; Bob, put your shoes on; Olson, exhausted, wants to go home to Constance and Kate; a cry in the dark: Olson, the flashlight, quick!; he runs and hands the flashlight to Cernovich: a beam picks out a head in the water; Twombly six meters out, up to his hips, out of breath; Rauschenberg farther out toward the middle, moaning, his voice breaking; Olson wraps up his coat, thinks of diving in, runs for the raft; Twombly turns back, beaten by the cold; Rauschenberg turns around; Twombly goes back toward him, cooing this way Bob, this way; blankets, a second flashlight, out of the water; Olson half carries him to the kitchen, the wet body against him; four men at the kitchen table ignore the scene, one smiling with passive pleasure; Twombly alone keeps his dignity, hunched silently over an electric stove; Olson goes to bed with cold ankles and falls asleep as if he had been in the lake Words: Twombly: they were really tearing it up / Bob, put your shoes on / this way Bob, this way; a cry: Olson, the flashlight, quick!; Olson to Creeley: he said he could not go any farther, that he could not get his breath back Atmosphere: pitch-dark night, snow, icy water, a trembling flashlight, adrenaline, dismay, Olson's revulsion at the wet body against him Stakes: a suicide attempt or a cry for attention from a man torn between his wife and the man he loves, before the eyes of the one who despises him and saves him
Josef teaches in the architecture department of the University of Havana (February 9-17). A summer trip to Mexico with a visit to the Maya ruins of Yucatán. Anni begins designing fabrics for Knoll.

The editor of Arts and Architecture writes to Ruth and Albert Lanier about the Laverne showroom in San Francisco and Ruth's folded papers. sentence: “there are great stories about Ruth's folded papers, whatever they are”
Olson–Leach–Wildenhain correspondence; crucial letters from Wildenhain (March 5, 1952) and Olson (March 8, 1952) on craft and education; Richards describes Leach as a father figure.

Isabel Guernsey points out to Albers wedges (wedge-shaped insertions) in the fabric, 11 feet 3 inches wide, during a visit on March 14, 1952. Exact date of March 14, 1952. Consequences: Albers sees in them possible signs of weaving carried out from both ends.
Archer had invited Walker Evans to come and teach photography at BMC; he politely declines in a telegram addressed to Hazel Larsen. telegram preserved in the Western Regional Archives, Box 39

Keller complains that the painting curriculum is rigged: views diverging from those of Dean Sawyer and department chairman Albers are frowned upon and removed; he denounces a curriculum that is personal and narrow, excluding everything but what a small number of men believe to be the only way. Letter of March 23, 1952, Griswold archives (RU 22), Yale library. Consequences: Shows the anxiety of the older teachers in the face of Albers's changes.

Olson thanks Wildenhain for her advice on the Alfred potters: Harder's strongest recommendation, backed by Robert Turner, was for Karen Karnes, but it is her husband David Weinrib who receives the official post — at Harder's suggestion — and the college gets both. Consequences: Reveals pay discrimination: Weinrib draws the salary for both years although Karnes is the appointed instructor

Letter from Sawyer to Schweikher; Schweikher accepted the chairmanship thanks to George Howe's relentless persuasion Schweikher, a 1929 graduate of Yale architecture, visiting critic since the fall of 1947

Pottery seminar from October 15 to 29, 1952: Wildenhain gives demonstrations, lectures, and debates with her international colleagues Hamada, Leach, and Yanagi. Consequences: A public confrontation with Leach

A two-week seminar paired with a fall Crafts Institute. Official flyer: a hundred dollars' registration fee for discussions, lectures, technical demonstrations by Leach, Hamada, and Wildenhain, and a lecture by Dr. Soetsu Yanagi, director of the Imperial Folk Museum in Tokyo. Seventeen professional potters, instructors, and a few amateurs enrolled from all over the country; local potters, Trude Guermonprez (a future teacher at the college), and Warren MacKenzie (a future summer teacher) also attend. 100 dollars' tuition; 17 enrolled; a poster announcing the themes: the development of form ideas, design for mass production, craft in the machine world, master and apprentice in the workshop and in college, the relation of craft to art Consequences: Gives the ceramics program a national identity; the conversations continue in a national tour by Leach, Hamada, and Yanagi the following year and in Craft Horizons and Ceramics Monthly
Letter from Leser to the Board announcing that the Rockefeller and Ford foundations refuse to fund the college. Consequences: Deepens the financial crisis
“A Statement on the New Institute Program,” a talk of four printed pages, given at the college. four printed pages

Albers proposes a course of basic exercises in construction, combination, and drawing, general rather than specialized in nature, with practical studies of the interaction of color; he does not separate two- and three-dimensional design and aims at training in observation and articulation, both perceptual and conceptual. Letter in English, owned by Nicolás Piwonka.
Piwonka describes his own course: exercises in observation and criticism; spatial organization on a single plane; relations of volumes. The pedagogical coincidences are obvious. Letter in English.

The first exhibition opens on March 3 in Rome, the second on March 14 in Florence; following the advice of a local critic, he throws most of the works into the Arno. It saved him the problem of packing Consequences: deliberate destruction of the works

Rauschenberg's first solo exhibition in Europe, from March 3 to 10, 1953, at the Galleria dell'Obelisco, accompanied by a statement explaining the choice of materials lasting one week; a printed statement on the choice of materials

Grace Hartigan notes in her diary that she is especially happy to see the de Koonings in the crowd at her solo show; nervous, she drinks half a pint of Scotch; after the drinks, everyone moves on to the cocktail party of the collector Roland Pease. half a pint of Scotch drunk by Hartigan

Hartigan, nervous, drinks half a pint of Scotch; she notes in her diary her joy at seeing the de Koonings; after the free drinks, the group moves on to the collector's cocktail party Atmosphere: euphoria, free liquor, the round of parties
The Alberses arrive in the country; Josef develops a course of twelve hours a week for about six weeks, plus curriculum advice and lectures at the university. 12 hours/week, about 6 weeks

Duncan writes a long letter analyzing the Rumaker case: Rumaker knows how to enter a story with taste and catch voices, but he must move from the journalism of the everyday to the great reaches of time; he cites Pound's question about telling the low from the high. The letter had been addressed to Olson (and Creeley). references to Ring Lardner, William Saroyan, Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Saint Francis (Brother Fire), Lorca via Blackburn, the magazine ORIGIN, the Analects of Confucius Consequences: Rumaker reads it as a perfectly posed statement that he is about to explore

Early in the morning, after a memorably rough crossing, the liner United States docks with Albers on board — twenty years almost to the day since Josef and Anni had left Germany amid great uncertainty. His younger sister Lisbet and her husband Rudolf Marx, who have come from Bottrop, wait for him on the dock; he has a meal with them before taking the train to Ulm. The liner United States; a rough crossing. Consequences: Albers's first return to Germany, as an American citizen.

In letters to Anni, Albers describes the landscape: the Münsterland, with its incredibly clean and neat houses; the industrial Ruhr, unchanged since his youth, dense and ugly, where the bombed houses seem to belong naturally to the landscape; the Rhine vineyards in orderly rows on the steep slopes, which remind him of Peru; the little hamlets on the Rhine, beautiful as a dream. A current of restrained excitement runs through his tone.

Early morning, after a very rough crossing, the liner United States docks; his younger sister and brother-in-law, who have come from Bottrop, wait on the dock; breakfast together, then the train to Ulm. Atmosphere: Dawn, the ship listing, a reserved reunion — twenty years almost to the day after the flight of 1933. Stakes: The return to his native land, as an American citizen.
Albers sends Anni a box of color cards; the box, made by Robert Engman, is preserved at the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation box made by Robert Engman

He describes to Anni a drive through the snowy winter landscape to Ottobeuren and its renowned Benedictine abbey, its basilica, and its great organ: a fantastically large and dramatic basilica; with no Mass, a magnificent organ, apparently a Benedictine monk letting loose a New Year's hallelujah, enough to leave one cold and weak, jaw dropped, before such powerful exaltation. A snowy landscape; the basilica and great organ of the Benedictine abbey.

A drive through the snowy landscape to the Benedictine abbey; a visit to the basilica; a monk, with no Mass, launches into a New Year's hallelujah on the organ. Words: Albers to Anni: it leaves one cold and weak, jaw dropping, before such powerful exaltation. Atmosphere: Snow, baroque immensity, unexpected organ music.
Takes part in this exhibition, a sequel to the Ninth Street Gallery exhibitions.

Einstein, approached (by the person mentioned in the postscript, presumably for support for the endangered college), writes a public statement: he has followed the development of Black Mountain College with keen interest for years, convinced that an education without a living personal relationship among all concerned is far from the ideal; the university must develop character and social cohesion, not merely transmit knowledge; small institutions must be encouraged, and mass production must be kept from extending to human beings themselves. Letter dated “January 16, 1954,” opening with “To whom it may concern”. Consequences: Dawson comments: the college failed only the failures, and not even all of them.

An American specialist's report on a course in basic drawing, design, and color given at the Hochschule für Gestaltung in Ulm; republished in 1967 as “My Courses at Hochschule für Gestaltung in Ulm” in Form.

Olson, after a trying month (illness, cold), answers Rumaker: he may come up for graduation in writing; he must declare a date, an interim committee will define the gaps to be filled and the level of writing required; Olson thinks Rumaker and Jorge Fick should be the first graduates of a writing department. start of the spring quarter set for March 29, 1954 Consequences: the official creation of a two-man writing “department”: Olson and Creeley

Creeley, having printed the first issue of The Black Mountain Review in Mallorca, sails for the United States on March 13, according to Olson's letter; he is expected at the college at the end of March 1954 to teach. date “March 13” noted by Olson; first issue of the Review printed in Mallorca Consequences: contagious excitement and anticipation at the college

Creeley leaves the Spanish island of Mallorca for the United States, as Olson's letter notes. Date noted as “March 13” in Olson's letter. Consequences: Expected at Black Mountain at the end of March 1954 to begin teaching.

Creeley, freshly moved, writes of his enthusiasm: the story is a real breakthrough (“the real break-through”); he plans to publish it, probably in issue 5 (spring); a long story by Larry Eigner fills issue 4. He advises reading Ford Madox Ford, Some Do Not. Casa Martina, Bonanova, Palma Consequences: For two days Rumaker's feet do not touch the ground; he rereads the letter again and again, then writes half a dozen stories

Premiere of the dance Minutiae: choreography by Merce Cunningham, music by John Cage, costumes by Remy Charlip, set by Rauschenberg — a freestanding stage construction made of the materials, techniques, and structures characteristic of his work of the period. Consequences: Revived at the Henry Street Playhouse on May 27, 1955, and at the Brooklyn Academy of Music on January 12, 1957; excerpts videotaped in mid-November 1976 for “Dance in America” (WNET)
Premiere of Minutiae: choreography by Merce Cunningham, music by John Cage, costumes by Remy Charlip, a freestanding set built by Rauschenberg.

A few weeks after the start of the Algerian War (November 1, 1954), the Surrealists join the Comité de lutte contre la répression coloniale; from 1954 to 1958 they belong to at least five committees for Algerian prisoners and draft resisters and contribute to the Comité d'action des intellectuels (cofounded by Breton). The war began on 1954-11-01. Consequences: A swift mobilization compared with that of other intellectuals (from mid-1955).

On the frozen morning of New Year's Eve, Rumaker takes the A train to the George Washington Bridge to hitchhike to New Jersey. In a riveted alcove at the base of the south cable, he finds an old drunk apparently frozen to death, purple and stiff to the touch, empty pint wine bottles around him; he tells himself someone will find him soon enough and goes on. It takes him all day to reach Exit 3 in short rides; on the winding ramp in the dark, a car of drunken soldiers on leave heading north from the South; the driver, a disgusted young soldier, tries to palm off on him a marine with a bandaged hand, drunker than the others, who lives in National Park; while calling the marine's father from a drugstore, Rumaker sees the son fighting violently with three passing soldiers. He takes mental notes for his notebook, with the cold eye of the future writer. The A train; an alcove of riveted steel at the base of the south cable; empty pint bottles; Exit 3 of the Turnpike; a drugstore; a notebook in his hip pocket. Consequences: Writing material noted in memory.

Crossing the bridge on foot on a freezing morning, Rumaker finds an old drunk apparently frozen to death, touches him — purple and stiff —, notes the empty pint bottles, tells himself someone will find him, and goes on toward the New Jersey Turnpike, shaken but already noting the details for his notebook Words: “Nothing can be done now… They'll find him soon enough” Atmosphere: Biting cold, numb fingers, the detachment of a writer in the making Stakes: The birth of the writer's cold eye
Christmas morning, an early knock at the door: Duncan announces that he is Williams's Christmas present. A small apartment at the back of a courtyard/garden
Rauschenberg organizes a Feldman concert on Christmas Day in the gallery, an event known since as “Morton Feldman Concert with Paintings”. a concert on Christmas Day

Early on Christmas morning, a knock at the door; Williams gets out of bed and opens it; Duncan presents himself as his Christmas present Words: “Well, here I am, I'm your Christmas Present” Atmosphere: A winter dawn, charmed surprise Stakes: The magus's charm, poetic friendship

Rauschenberg organizes a Feldman concert on Christmas Day amid his red paintings on display Atmosphere: contemporary music and painting in an empty gallery on December 25 Stakes: the fusion of disciplines, an echo of BMC in New York

With Herb gone back to Houston, Merrill turns up at Ben's with a pint of whiskey and invites Rumaker to Times Square. An immense crowd, hundreds of thousands of drunks in paper hats; the human pressure, a current that threatens to sweep them away, frightens them; they work their way to a side street and then to Bryant Park (a major cruising ground at the time), behind the Fifth Avenue library, and finish the whiskey on a bench to the sound of horns, sirens, and gunshots. Back at Ben's in the early morning, in Ben's big bed, Merrill gets from Rumaker, calmed by the whiskey, what he had always wanted at Black Mountain: first penetration, sharp pain and then pleasure, tinged with Catholic guilt and shame, Rumaker determined that Ben must never find out. A pint of whiskey; hundreds of thousands of people; paper hats, horns; horns and shotgun blasts in the distance. Consequences: The last virginity overcome; the affair with Merrill reborn.

Merrill appears at Ben's with a pint of whiskey; Rumaker frozen in the doorway, then accepts; a crushing crowd; panic at being swept away; a struggle toward a side street; a bench in Bryant Park where they finish the bottle to the sound of the celebrations. Atmosphere: Physical terror of the human current sweeping them away; drunkenness; shared relief on the bench. Stakes: The rebirth of the affair and Rumaker's reassertion of himself as a rebel and “queer” writer.

A letter reproduced in full: Rumaker announces that he is resuming his Shakespeare tutorial (Richard II, then Hamlet), wants to begin Chaucer with Olson in the spring, and aims to graduate in June 1955; he describes the IBM job (a view of the East River and the UN, a big office, THINK signs — some wit has written “REFLEXIONE” by hand in place of the typewriter lost after the breakup with Ben), the in-house paper IBM World Trade News, his colleagues (a young Italian woman who dabbles in poetry, a wound-up Dutchman who types with two fingers, pencil clenched, a former writer of stories in Dutch, both bored to death; she has lived in Mallorca and is fascinated by BMC — perhaps all three of them will go back), the New York gossip against Olson (“stutterer,” “infantile talent,” incoherent, “no logic in his imagination”) that makes him angry, and sends his greetings to Connie and Kate. Consequences: Confirms the planned return to BMC at the end of March.

A panel responding to O'Hara's essay arguing for a broad notion of “nature” that includes abstraction; in it O'Hara writes that Elaine's basketball players “leap in excitement of paint” like the cheers of the spectators and that what she feels goes straight onto the canvas

Rumaker sends the rewrite of his story about boredom (Irvington and a students' lounge), renamed The Jest, with a new character, Finchley, Irvington's brother. He describes his method: letting the characters speak and act without any preconceived notion, never knowing what is coming — which excites him and makes him feel “wide-open”. He says he has read Richard II and is preparing a paper; a poor borrowed typewriter, a dreadful carbon, irony about “the big majah,” gone to the Greek consulate. carbon copy; a poor-quality borrowed typewriter; an IBM electric typewriter used at work in the boss's absence

Olson officially announces that the turn has come, and it is forward: the college will operate for the spring and summer quarters. Rumaker, Tom, Jerry, and Ed are the solid ones, the core around which to build, with only students who are “sharp and directed”. There are no more scholarships; Rumaker can get a loan from the Derek Bovingdon fund until he graduates. Strict admission requirements: (1) to know what one wants and to fit what the college can give; (2) to have one-third of $850 per quarter. An ironic mention of Rumaker's literary friends who added Keats and Shelley to Swinhall. A handwritten postscript: his mother has written a “damn nice letter” about the college's Appeal. $850 per quarter; one-third to be had in hand; sale of livestock, plows, property; Appeal sent to friends and families; the lower half of the campus not yet sold; Bovingdon loan at a minimum annual interest of 6% Consequences: Rumaker's plan to return in the spring/summer of 1955; Rumaker's surprise that his mother was moved

Discouraged by the tuition to be paid and the silence about “The Pipe,” Rumaker writes that he does not know whether he will come back. Olson replies on Black Mountain Review letterhead, shaken by Rumaker's closing sentence: “What is this?” letterhead: The Black Mountain Review, Black Mountain, North Carolina Consequences: a dramatic cliffhanger over the return

Rumaker, who has to pay his tuition and has heard nothing from Olson about “The Pipe,” writes that he is ready to give it all up; Olson replies on Black Mountain Review letterhead that he must not let the Bovingdon loan frighten him: after two years, paying the 6% interest (36 dollars a year) is enough to acknowledge the debt. He insists on Rumaker, Tom, Ed, and Jerry as the hard core of the college and apologizes for being unable to read the manuscripts, taken up as he is with trucks, cows, plumbing, tables, chairs, and refrigerators — a junk dealer of the remaining property, keeping the school afloat. letterhead “The Black Mountain Review, Black Mountain, North Carolina”; 6% interest, $36/year; trucks, cows, plumbing, tables, chairs, iceboxes Consequences: Rumaker returns for the spring quarter

Creeley judges “Exit 3” (sent with “The Jest”) the best, with “potential”: he would like it tightened; he likes the detail of the woman washing the drugstore window and the four soldiers; the secondary character is too much of an “on-looker,” now inside, now outside — a “mobile lamp-post”. He adds that the magazine is precarious, a question of money; it will probably become biannual, 150-175 pages, in a smaller format. magazine planned as biannual, circa 150/175 pp., a smaller format; drugstore, four soldiers

On Black Mountain Review paper, Olson answers Rumaker's discouraged letter, shaken by the sentence saying he does not know whether he will come back to the college: “What is this?” Words: “What is this? Or at least, do let us…” Atmosphere: affectionate, vehement concern Stakes: Rumaker's return, and with it the survival of the college's core

Creeley likes “the invention,” the “break-over” into a world where things draw their own logic; he remembers taking longer than Rumaker to get there, having stayed too much in the autobiographical. Criticisms: condense the lead-in; the two “tales” (Carp and his forks, Billy and the baby) are the center and “lift very wildly”; the conversation is very good; cut after the fight, close short and sharp, laconic. Postscript: “That pipe is a beautifully handled image.” He mentions Olson's telegram — “the mag was 'safe'” — and signs “All love, Bob”. Olson's telegram on the rescue of the magazine; the tales of Carp (the forks) and Billy (the baby) Consequences: Rumaker's talent confirmed in the eyes of his second mentor

Wes has Rumaker sign an IOU: $287.50 to be repaid two years after his last date of attendance, at 2% annual interest, 6% if late. The loan covers his tuition and lets him finish his degree. Amount: $287.50; interest 2%, then 6%; signed “Michael Rumaker, March 29, 1955” Consequences: Rumaker can graduate but worries about repayment
Howe's death; according to Stern, it helped the university's wish to pass over the conflicts in silence; Howe had supported Nalle and Schweikher in his report

Albers arrives in Ulm and writes to Anni on May 20 of his impression of the new campus, which he will later call an imposing complex of buildings; he teaches twenty-six students there Words: a description of the campus in his daily letters Atmosphere: a German summer course, a love correspondence at a distance Stakes: Albers's return to Germany, twelve years after fleeing the Nazis — on a former concentration-camp site

Frightened and confused by the assigned tasks and the formal requirements of graduation, Rumaker types a long letter to Olson: he has wasted the quarter; Shakespeare has become inaccessible to him — like a pane of glass between him and the plays —; he feels like a toad, very vacant but troubled; he dreads the oral examination before the whole faculty (his mind panics under direct questioning); he would like to go on to graduate school in order to teach; and he asks what remains to be done before the end of the summer. Typed on Merrill's old upright piano; plans to read Richard II and Hamlet; graduation planned for the end of summer 1955.

One afternoon, frightened by the tasks and the graduation procedure, Rumaker types a long letter to Charles: a wasted quarter, Shakespeare like a window he can see through but not get past, emptiness broken by brief bursts of activity — in between he squats like a toad; terror of the oral before the faculty; plans for graduate school and teaching; a request to know what remains to be done before the end of the summer. Words: “it's like a funny kind of plateglass window stands between me and them”; “in between I squat like a toad - very vacant, yet troubled”. Atmosphere: An austere room, the stream outside, the student's solitary anguish. Stakes: Taking stock of an education as the college dies out.
Forced to borrow $50 more from the college itself, on the same terms, which allows him to stay until early September. $50, June 13, 1955 Consequences: His stay extended until early September 1955

An informal ceremony and party: Olson, as rector, has asked Joe Fiore, the art instructor, to hand-letter an honorary diploma in the field of writing — a request made that same afternoon, which annoys Joe, who complains that he does not have enough time. Richard is absent. Olson presents the diploma with a grand gesture and his broadest smile, proudly announcing that he has had “Summa cum laude” inscribed in blue letters, with a look as if asking to be forgiven for something. Rumaker, exhausted, stays gloomy and silent, exasperated above all by Wolpe's voice, shrill in his ears that evening. Rumaker still wears dressings reduced to the size of large adhesive bandages; “Summa cum laude” in blue letters; Wolpe's voice, usually inventive, loud with spontaneous atonal phrasings. Consequences: Rumaker knows it is definitely time to leave Black Mountain.

An informal graduation party; Joe Fiore, annoyed by the last-minute request, has hand-lettered the diploma; Olson presents it with a grand gesture and his broadest smile, announcing the “Summa cum laude” in blue letters, his eyes seeking Rumaker's as if to make up for something; Rumaker, bandaged, stays silent, physically holding himself to his chair so as not to flee, Wolpe's voice piercing his ears. Words: Olson proudly announces the “Summa cum laude”; Joe complains about the lack of time. Atmosphere: Good humor on one side, nervous exhaustion on the other; distress beneath the party. Stakes: The departure: it was definitely time to leave Black Mountain.

The day after Rumaker's graduation, Duncan writes from Mallorca to accompany his letter of recommendation on Rumaker: he recognizes the young writer's qualities, a Rumaker universe, but admits his impatience with his way of writing; he distinguishes the educational level (Rumaker writes better than the average graduate) from what he calls Learning, as opposed to colleges and universities; he quotes Pound, urges Olson to discover his Maximus, calls on Lorca via Blackburn and the formula about technique, work, and the absolute account of what a poem is. Dated “Banalbufar, Mallorca, September 6, 1955,” addressed to “Dear Charles / Dear Bob” (Olson and Creeley); mention of an issue of ORIGIN that arrived the day before with Blackburn's translations of Lorca.
